p: In Pueblo her father finally told the story of his hand.
Ernie's crew tested the line at the switch and called it dead, but a farm generator was feeding it backward, and Frank climbed without his own tester or grounds.
Nadia and Callie fought over the dishes about whose check you trust, and Callie drove off with Rosie that night.
Back at FRO the stand-in rack went into HEARTH, and Nadia found both cabin relief valves sitting behind one manual valve with a red handle, carried over from cargo.
Wes put his hand on the handle next to hers, and neither of them let go.
Wes Harland. Chief engineer. The red valve in the relief line is his.
Tiago Ferreira. Test lead. He just slid the stand-in rack into HEARTH.
Odette. Safety engineer. She owns the overpressure hazard report.
Amara Osei. Program manager, still counting every week and dollar.
Gus. Test cell technician. He walked the stand-in up the ramp.
Ines. FRO's quality manager. She audited both ends of the seal order.

Wes's truck was in the lot at ten to seven on Friday, parked inside the lines for once. Half the high bay lights were still on night mode. She found him inside HEARTH at the relief plate by the hatch, cargo drawings rolled under one arm, pencil behind his ear, same shirt as yesterday.

He didn't say good morning. I went through all eleven cargo sets, he said. Every place a manual valve sits in front of something that's supposed to work by itself. There's one more. The cabin pressure transducers. Same valve, same tag, so we could leak test the port. He flicked the red handle with a fingernail. It didn't move. Twenty years I've been putting these in.
He'd drawn the fix in pencil on the back of a cargo drawing. The red valve was gone. The two relief valves bolted straight onto the tee, and the tee onto the one fitting through the shell.
Cargo had one hole, and I'm keeping it, he said. I'm losing the handle.
Tiago pulls both valves and plugs the ports. Proof, leak, then the valves go back on and get their own leak check in place.
And the night somebody leaves a plug in.
She heard it as it came out. Three weeks back, at her father's sink, dish towel in hand, she'd said it nearly word for word, and Callie had dropped the towel on the counter.

Wes didn't argue. Tiago did. He'd come in early too, and was leaning in the hatch with a coffee from the gas station on Arapahoe. Then the plug's got a handle on it as long as my forearm, painted red, he said. Make it so the vent cap won't go on with a plug in. You can't close the plate over one. Wes looked at him, then wrote it on the drawing.
It was Callie's answer with a wrench in it. Build it so the crew won't let him up. Nadia kept that to herself.

Odette came up at nine and rewrote HR-22 at the HEARTH room table. The two relief valves would share only the tee and the fitting through the shell, passive metal, covered the way the shell itself was covered: design for minimum risk, big margins, proved at proof pressure with everything else. The plugs went on the closeout list as ground items. Two people would sign that both were out before the plate closed for flight.
Two valves, two plugs, two names, she said, and wrote that across the bottom of the page.

The product baseline had been under the board since CDR, so the fix would go in as a change request. Wes wrote it himself, with the transducer valve on the same page, and put his own name in the box for the requester. Then he rolled the cargo drawings up and tucked them back under his arm.
It was one valve, he said.

Monday of week twenty five Tiago's integration sequence covered most of the wall in his office off the high bay: twenty one steps, from the first breaker in HEARTH's power distribution to the rack making air. The stand-in had been in its bay since Thursday, six hundred kilograms of steel ballast with Tamarack's connectors on its back.
The real rack would reach the high bay next week and go into HEARTH the week after. Proof testing started in week twenty nine.

Two weeks of steps on a steel box, Amara said. Then we do them again on the real one. Tell me why I'm paying twice. Wes, from the doorway: Put the rack in first when it gets here. It's the one that's late. Build around it.

The twenty one steps fall into four stages, and each stage ends with a check before the next one starts. The stand-in holds the rack's place through the first three. For the data stage Jun writes a simulator that answers on HEARTH's network the way the rack's controller will. Nothing that can be proven on the steel box waits for the real one. It gets proven early, where a fault can only be in the last thing added. Amara takes back four days by running checkouts on a second shift.

Integration order follows dependencies, and incremental build-up checks each step so a new fault usually sits in the last element added. Stand-ins and simulators are enabling systems that let integration start before every element is ready.

Tuesday the harness shop's lead caught Nadia at the shop door with a spool in each hand. The stand-in's harnesses had come off his pegboards two weeks back, built from the shop's cargo stock, which was fine for a steel box that would never leave the ground. Now he was building the flight set, and the wire the drawings called for had run out four harnesses short.
The supplier quoted five weeks. On his shelf sat two thousand meters of cargo wire, same gauge, same color code. He held that spool up. It had flown, he said, and he could have the set done Friday.

Nadia asks Jun what a crewed cabin needs from its wire before anyone cuts a length. He has the answer by lunch. HEARTH's cabin wire has to pass the crewed cabin flammability and offgassing tests, and the cargo wire's insulation was never tested to that standard. Cargo modules weren't built for people to live in. The harness lead calls distributors while Jun finds an equal on the approved list. A warehouse in Aurora has eight hundred meters of it, three days out. The shop builds those four last, and each traveler says which reel.
Implementation builds to the design. When a material can't be had as specified, the question goes back to design definition, which decides whether a substitute meets the design's characteristics.

The board approved Wes's change on Tuesday. Wednesday morning Gus cut the safety wire and lifted the red valve out of the relief line, and Wes asked for it. It went on the shelf over his desk with its tag still on. Jun took a kilogram and a half off the mass roll-up. Every kilogram counted now, on a margin of about 800.

Amara wanted the relief tee written up as a lesson learned before the week was out. FRO's lessons learned lived in a shared folder: two hundred and fourteen documents, the newest eight years old. Tiago said he'd opened it once, to see if it existed.

Lessons learned is where a lesson goes to die, Wes said. I've got all of these, and they're up here. He tapped his temple with the pencil. If a second module ever came, Osprey's or anyone's, it would start from HEARTH's drawings.

Nadia puts it where the next designer will trip on it. FRO's design review checklist gets a line: no single manual valve, plug or cap in the path of controls meant to work alone. The standard relief drawing loses its valve. The lesson gets one paragraph with the cargo history, the fix, Odette's name and Wes's. Then Jun asks Wes for an hour a week to walk the cargo drawings with a recorder running. Wes says two hours, and bring coffee.

Knowledge management makes knowledge reusable across the organization: lessons turned into standards, checklists and training, and know-how that lives in experienced people's heads drawn out and kept.

Thursday Tiago walked Nadia and FRO's facilities manager through the pressure test cell. HEARTH's proof test was set for week twenty nine. The cell had been built for cargo modules, and the facilities manager had kept it running since the first one.

Tiago had his list on a clipboard. The nitrogen line into the cell was sized for a cargo module, and HEARTH's ninety cubic meters would take fourteen hours to fill. The cell's pressure gauges came due for calibration the week after proof, and the calibration lab was booked three weeks out. The compressor's yearly service sat on the facilities calendar the same week as proof. A second module, if one came, would want the same cell the year after.
The cell had run fine for eleven modules, the facilities manager said. He wanted to know what was different.

Tiago's clipboard turns into a page: what HEARTH needs from the cell, week by week, through ship. The compressor service moves to next week. The gauges go to the calibration lab in two weeks, good through ship, not just through proof. A bigger nitrogen line goes on the facilities plan for the winter shutdown, with a trailer to cover HEARTH until then. The facilities manager adds the cell to the page he shows FRO's board every quarter, with HEARTH's dates and a blank row for the next module.

Infrastructure management provides and maintains the facilities, equipment and services projects need, across the life cycle. It plans capacity and upkeep from the projects' needs, at the organization's level.

Colleen's airplane was getting a second radio, a backup to the one put in that spring. On Saturday of week twenty five Nadia found her at the avionics shop at Erie, watching a technician build the harness on a pegboard: a nail at every branch, the drawing taped above it, each wire cut, labeled and tied in place long before it went near the airplane.
She builds it on the board so it fits in the panel, Colleen said. You don't want to find a short wire behind the instruments. Then, without looking up from the pegboard: How's your sister?
Fine. Colleen let that sit, and went back to watching the wires.

With the radio in, the technician pulled every circuit breaker, powered the radio alone, then pushed the others in one by one with a headset on, listening for a whine. Turn it all on at once and hear noise, Colleen said, and you've got nine suspects.

The shop had one test bench, booked by three airplanes that week, and every gauge on it carried a calibration sticker with a date. The shop decides what benches it owns, Colleen said. My airplane just has to be on the schedule.

Before the airplane left, the shop's inspector wrote the radio into the logbook: what came out, what went in, the serial numbers, his signature. The airplane is whatever the logbook says, Colleen said, plus anything somebody forgot to write. The next mechanic only gets the first part.

Sunday she didn't call. She drove down instead, without telling anybody, because the word fine, said to Colleen over a pegboard, had ridden around in her head all night. Callie worked Sunday days at the utility's control center, a low tan building off the interstate north of Pueblo with no sign on it and a fence that went all the way around.

She texted from the lot. Callie came out to the gate in a fleece with the utility's logo on it, her badge on a lanyard, and looked at her through the chain link for a long second. You drove two hours to sit in a parking lot.

Callie went back inside and phoned her supervisor. Ten minutes later Nadia was signing a visitor log, locking her phone in a gray locker, and following her sister down a hall that smelled like carpet cleaner and burnt coffee.

The room was dim and cool and quieter than she'd pictured. A wall of screens at the front drew the whole county as lines and boxes, green where a line was energized and white where it wasn't. Callie's desk had three monitors, two phones, a radio handset on a coiled cord, and a photo of Rosie taped to one bezel. She pointed Nadia at a rolling chair by the back wall. Visitors sit there. Visitors don't talk while I'm keyed up.

At twenty to eleven a crew called in from a county road east of town. A crossarm had cracked on a pole, and they needed the line it carried out of service to change it. Callie already had the switching order. She'd written it Friday, she said without turning around, and somebody else on the floor had checked it Saturday, because nobody checks their own.

She keyed the radio and read it out: which switch, open, tagged. A switchman twelve miles away read it back to her word for word, opened it, and called back when it was open and his tag was hung with his name on it. Callie typed the time. Then she called the crew. Switch forty four seventeen is open and tagged, she said. You're clear to test and ground.

Nadia waited for the word, and it didn't come. The crew lead read the clearance back. Callie asked him where he'd test, and he told her: at the pole, on the wire he'd be working. A minute later he called it dead where he stood. Then he called in his grounds, one on each side of the work, each by the number stenciled on its clamp. Callie typed both numbers into a box on her screen, and two small red tags came up on the county map at that pole.
When it went quiet Nadia rolled her chair a foot closer. You didn't say dead.
I don't. Callie didn't look away from the map. I can see the switch. I can't see his wire. I tell him what I know, and he finds out the rest where he's standing.
Callie gave her a look over the top of her monitor that was all their father. Who do you think.
Nadia nodded at the two red tags. And those?

His grounds. They stay on my screen till he calls each one off, by number. That switch doesn't close while there's a red tag up there. Not for me, not for my boss, not for anybody. She tapped the box with a pen. The switchman can be wrong. I can be wrong. His tester can be wrong. You don't trust any one of us. You hook us together so it takes all three being wrong on the same morning.

Nadia sat back in the visitor chair. Three checks, three people, three places, none of them leaning on the others, and a screen that remembered every clamp hung on a wire until it came off. Nobody in the room made that crew safe. The way the room was hooked together did. She'd driven down to watch one call, and there wasn't one.

At ten past two the new crossarm was up. The crew lead called his grounds off one at a time, by number, and Callie cleared each red tag as he said it. Only when the box was empty did she call the switchman to close forty four seventeen. The road east of town went green on the wall again.
Callie walked her out to the gate with her hands in her fleece pockets. So, she said. Now you've seen one.

I know it's good. Callie looked off toward the interstate. You still drove down to check my work. Nadia didn't have an answer that wasn't yes. Callie nodded like that settled something and went back in through the gate without turning around.

She didn't stop at her father's. She'd have had to say why she came. Somewhere past Fountain the family thread lit up with a photo, no caption: the first red tomato off the plants out back, held up in both of Rosie's hands. At the next exit Nadia typed three replies, deleted them, and sent a heart.

Monday the flight harnesses started coming off the shop's pegboards. Each label carried a drawing number and a dash. The rack's power harness was W-114, and its data harness was W-117. The dash said which set: dash one for the stand-in's set, built from cargo wire, and dash three for flight. On the cargo modules the shop had tested harnesses after they were installed, all of them in one day.
Testing them installed saved a day on the bench, the harness lead said. They'd always done it that way.

Nadia has the shop test each harness on the bench. Every wire gets continuity and insulation resistance there, where a fault costs a re-crimp instead of a day inside the module. Each harness leaves with a traveler: drawing, dash number, serial, wire reel, crimp tool, the tester's name, and the numbers. Jun asks the shop to wrap the stand-in's harnesses in yellow tape at both ends, so they can't be mistaken for flight.

Implementation realizes each element and records the evidence: what it was built from, how, by whom, and how it tested. Checking an element before integration keeps faults out of the assembly, and the record travels with the part.

The rack came down from Frederick on Tuesday of week twenty six in a box truck, and Irena rode in the cab with her own torque wrench on her lap. She'd built most of its frame. Her week at the lake started the Thursday after first power.

It sat in the high bay on its dolly under a clean tent. Tiago had the install for Monday and first power for Tuesday. The stand-in had carried Tamarack's own connectors since it went in, and every one of them had mated.
Connectors fit, Tiago said. Do I need more than that?

Jun builds the checklist from the interface control document, the ICD, line by line. Every pin at HEARTH's harness ends. Voltage at the connector with a load on it. The rack's chassis bond to its mounts. Coolant pressure and flow at the quick disconnects, with water at temperature. On the rack's side, its connector pinouts against the same pages. Everything checks. One question goes on the open list: the ICD says how the rack's chassis bonds to HEARTH, and nothing about where the data cable's shield is grounded.

Integration checks each interface against its definition before elements are joined, so a mismatch shows up as a reading, not as damage. Fit isn't function, and the interface document is the reference.

Friday FRO's flight software lead brought HEARTH's half of the rack software to Tiago's integration meeting. Her team had been working in sprints since week thirteen. The newest build on her branch had a fix in it from Wednesday, for a command signing timeout they'd hit in the lab. She'd load whatever was newest Tuesday morning, she said. Every day it was better.

Nadia asks for a tagged release instead of whatever's newest. Version 0.9.2 is tagged Friday afternoon with Wednesday's fix in it, and released to integration the controlled way: a named version, approved, with a record of what's in it. Four hundred and twelve unit tests, all passing. Three known issues, each with a workaround, on one page. The integration log records the version and the file's checksum. On Tuesday, when the panel says 0.9.2, everyone in the bay knows exactly what that is.

Implementing a software element ends in a defined, tested release: built from a known version, unit tested, documented and recorded, so integration knows exactly which element it has. Configuration management's release control governs what gets released and when.

Monday of week twenty seven the real rack went into its bay. By noon HEARTH's integration had produced a binder of as-run procedures in Tiago's pencil, three hundred photos on Gus's phone, and the model check results on Jun's laptop.
Irena had brought Tamarack's acceptance data on a thumb drive, every page stamped proprietary.
At two Helen called. Halo wanted to see HEARTH's integration data as it came in, and Halo's sustaining engineers would need it for fifteen years after that.

Jun and Tiago set up the integration record that afternoon. Every as-run procedure, photo and anomaly report gets an ID, a date, and the configuration it was taken on. Gus's photos go in named by step. Halo gets a view of everything FRO owns. Tamarack's pages stay marked, visible only to the people Pavel's agreement names. The plan says who keeps it, in what format, and for how long: fifteen years, then the station's end of life.

Information management plans what information a project creates and receives, how it's identified, stored, protected and shared, who can reach it, and how long it's kept. Other parties' protected data is handled on their terms.

Tuesday evening, with the rack mated, Tiago stood at the power panel with the procedure clipped open. The power harness, W-114, ran down from the overhead channel, and the data harness, W-117, ran beside it. Both were flight harnesses, off the shop's bench the week before. Irena stood at the rack's front face, where the controller's screen would come up.
The stand-in's been powered forty times, Tiago said. How careful do you want this?

The power card comes up at ten percent current limit, then half, then full. The controller boots. The fans go to low speed, then high. At every hold Jun reads the numbers against the band he predicted, and each one sits inside it. At twenty to nine the rack is pulling cabin air through its sorbent beds in its own bay. Tiago writes the time on the procedure's last page. Irena hasn't moved from the front face. When the fans step up to high she lays her palm flat on the frame she built and keeps it there until the CO2 number on the screen starts to fall.
First power of an integrated element goes in steps, with limits and expected values at each, so an interface fault shows up small and early. Integration checks the elements together, in place.
Tiago had been running two shifts since the rack went in. When first shift came on Wednesday, second shift had left a page on the clipboard.

The anomaly report on the rack bay, still open. The rack controller dropped off HEARTH's network nine times in fourteen hours, four to six seconds each, and every drop came within two seconds of the rack fans stepping up to high speed. The setup was the real rack, the flight power and data harnesses, and flight software 0.9.2. CO2 removal pauses during each drop, and the rack recovers on its own.
Gus, the test cell technician, already had a spare harness over his shoulder. Start swapping? he asked.

Tiago puts the rack in standby. Jun photographs every connector and writes each harness into the report by dash number and serial. On the whiteboard they list what could cause it: power noise, the data harness, the controller, the software. Jun turns that into a numbered plan, one change per step, each with what it should show and how to put it back. Gus initials each step as he does it. By four the drops follow fan speed and nothing else. Jun pulls both drawings. Tamarack grounds the data cable's shield at the rack. HEARTH's drawing grounds it at both ends. Two grounds and a fan motor make a loop.

When integration hits an anomaly, make the system safe, record the configuration, and investigate from a plan, one change at a time. The cause comes before the fix, and every change is recorded so it can be undone.
Wednesday night second shift put the stand-in's data harness into the rack bay, the cargo wire one. It grounded the shield at HEARTH's end only, the old cargo way. It was step six on Jun's plan.

By Thursday morning the rack had run eleven hours with its fans on high and hadn't dropped once. Irena had seen it as soon as Jun showed her HEARTH's drawing. Tamarack had always grounded its shields at the rack. She'd pushed her lake week back two days to watch the night run, and didn't mention it.
It works, Tiago said. Proof test's in two weeks. Leave it in, and make the drawing match.

By noon the as-built list says the stand-in's data harness is installed, temporary, with a red tag on the harness itself. A change request grounds the shield at HEARTH's end only, on the drawing and in a new ICD revision that finally says how both sides handle shields. The board approves it Friday. The shop builds a new flight data harness to that drawing on Monday, with a new dash number of its own. It goes in Tuesday, and the list changes again that afternoon.

Configuration management keeps the record matching the hardware. A change found in integration gets a change request, an impact assessment and a board decision; the baseline and interface documents are updated, and status accounting records what's installed at every step.

Monday of week twenty eight Odette needed one thing before she'd sign HEARTH into the proof test: that the module in the cell would be the module on the drawings. Ines came up from quality to ask the same question her own way.
Brannock's fifteen year aging result on the long cure lot was due Friday.
What's in it? Ines asked. Not what's on the list. What's in it.

Jun and Ines plan it for next Monday, the day before the proof test starts: every item on the as-built list found in the module, its label and serial read, its drawing and revision checked. Ines wants two people on each check and no one checking their own work. A functional audit against the requirements goes on the plan for the end of testing.

A physical configuration audit confirms the item as built matches its design documents, by looking at the hardware. A functional audit confirms it performs as required. Status accounting alone checks the records against each other.

Friday of week twenty eight Gus was putting the troubleshooting kit back in the cage. Nadia was at Tiago's desk with the proof test procedure, her phone face down beside it, because Brannock's result was due by five.

Gus came out of the cage with a harness coiled in a clear bag, its traveler folded inside. He set it on the desk between the procedure and her phone. Nadia turned the bag until the label came around. W-114, dash three. The rack's flight power harness.
Pulled it myself, Gus said. Wednesday, end of my shift. I was going to put it back first thing.

Power had been the first branch on the whiteboard. He'd put in the stand-in's harness to rule it out, nothing changed, and he'd bagged the flight one so it wouldn't get stepped on. That night the drops stopped, and there was never a next step. It was on Jun's plan in Gus's initials. Step four: swap in the stand-in's power harness, no change. Step five: put the flight one back. Step five had nothing beside it. Step six had second shift's initials. Jun's drawings had pointed at the shield by four, and second shift had gone straight to it.

Nadia opened the as-built list on her laptop. Power harness, flight, installed in week twenty seven. It said exactly what should have been there. The data harness had changed twice in a week, and both changes were on the list. The power harness had never been changed on purpose, so it had never been changed at all.

In the rack bay, under the overhead channel's cover, the rack's power ran through the stand-in's harness, built for a steel box of ballast, out of cargo wire. Nadia had turned that wire away herself a few weeks back, for a crewed cabin. It had yellow tape at both ends. Second shift had worked beside it Tuesday putting in the new data harness, and nobody looks twice at a harness that isn't the problem.
It's run clean all week, Tiago said.
On cargo wire. Ines's walk-down was Monday. It would have turned up then.

The night somebody leaves a plug in. She'd said it to Callie over the dishes. It hadn't been a plug, and the man who'd left it was the one who carried it out of the cage. On Callie's screen a ground stayed red until somebody called it off by number. Nothing in HEARTH had kept that count for a harness. Callie would have something to say about that. Nadia didn't know yet what she'd say back.
Gus looked back at the cage. There was a seal in a bag on that shelf for two years once, he said. This one's been nine days.
